seed: Shannon Byrne Susko, CULTURAL: Team Core Values Discovery, and Discovering or Confirming your Team Core Values with your Whole Leadership Team (adapted from Jim Collins’ Mission to Mars), Metronomics. Byron Darlison, Values: How Not To Chase Your Tail (darlison.com).

slides.title: Who would you send to Mars?
slides.headline: Who would you send to Mars?
slides.support: The Martians want to meet the people who best show what is right, best and noble about your company.
body: They learn your values only by watching those people live them.
notes: This is the Mission to Mars exercise. It discovers the values the company already lives.
It is for a team with no agreed Core Values, or one whose values failed the test. A team whose values passed the test skips it.
At Q2, teach the exercise. The leadership team then runs it with the whole company before the next session.
In a small company, the leadership team is most or all of the company. That company runs Mission to Mars in the room at Q3. Add these slides to that client’s Q3 deck. Allow about 60 minutes.

artwork.alt: Three neutral gray figures stand beside a small rocket. A fourth figure holds a clipboard and gestures toward them, choosing who boards. One of the three wears a green badge.

slides.title: Mission to Mars has five steps.
slides.headline: Mission to Mars has five steps.
notes: Walk the five steps once, so the leaders see where the exercise ends.
The leadership team runs these five steps in one session, with the whole company if you can.

artwork.alt: Five steps in a row. 1, pick three people. Each person picks three people and names the value each one lives. 2, share and cluster. Each person says who they picked and why. Move similar values together and name each cluster. 3, vote: three votes each, on the clusters that best show your values. 4, test the top three: test each one and talk about anything left out. 5, agree on the Core Values: name each value and write the behavior it means.

slides.title: Pick three people.
slides.headline: Pick three people.
slides.support: Work on your own. Pick three people who are not in this room.
body: Beside it, write the value that person lives.
Add one example of them living it.
notes: Each leader works in private. Show your answers, then agree.
The people must be outside the room, so nobody picks a colleague at the table.
Ask for behavior the leader has seen, not a quality they admire in general.

slides.title: Share who you picked, and why.
slides.headline: Share who you picked, and why.
slides.support: Each leader says who they picked and why.
body: Name each cluster with a word or a phrase.
notes: The coach groups the notes as each leader presents.
A few words that describe the behavior are enough for now. The names come at the end.

slides.title: Vote for the values that best show your company.
slides.headline: Vote for the values that best show your company.
body: Stack them on one cluster, or spread them.
notes: Tally the votes for each cluster. The three with the most votes go forward.

slides.title: Read your Core Values aloud.
slides.headline: Read your Core Values aloud.
slides.support: In Metronome: open One Page Plans.
body: Read each value and the behavior it means.
notes: At a quarterly, the team arrives in one of three places. It has agreed Core Values, a draft from a Mission to Mars session, or neither.
With agreed values, read them from the One Page Plan and go straight to the test.
With a draft, the leadership team reviews it, changes what needs changing and confirms it today.
With neither, say so. Agree on a date for the Mission to Mars session and move on.
The Core Values are what each leader rates their direct reports against on the A-Player grid.

slides.title: A Core Value is a name and the behavior it means.
slides.headline: A Core Value is a name and the behavior it means.

panels.heading: Honesty
panels.support: Tell the truth. Especially to yourself.

panels.heading: Persistence
panels.support: When blocked, dig in. Get creative. Get it done.

panels.heading: Reliability
panels.support: Do what you say. Every time.

notes: These are example Core Values. Use them to show the form: a short name, then the behavior it means.
Do not recommend adopting them. The team’s values are its own.
Watch for a value with no clear behavior behind it.

slides.title: Confirm your Core Values.
slides.headline: Confirm your Core Values.
slides.support: Change only what failed the test.
body: Each value has a name and the behavior it means.
They describe how your best people already act.
notes: A team with agreed values changes only what failed the test.
A team with a draft agrees on the name and the behavior today. The wording does not have to be perfect. Refine the words as homework.
Homework: share the Core Values with the whole company.

slides.title: Go deeper on Core Values before the next session.
slides.headline: Go deeper on Core Values before the next session.
notes: Scan to open each page on darlison.com.
The article shows how to describe each value at three levels of behavior. It also shows how to hire on the values.
The prompt pressure-tests each value against real stories. Its page is for members. The article How to Discover Your Company’s Values Using AI explains the prompt and is open to everyone.
